_doc: The rules of the Prairie Avenue DISTRICT DRAFT (owner, 2026-10-08; T-2159, split to T-2329 and T-2330; T-2160, split to T-2334 and T-2335; T-2161, split to T-2351 and T-2352). tools/draft_prairie_1904.py reads this file, the traced Sanborn footprints (data/traces/prairie_1904_footprints_s<sheet>.json), the sheet census and the T-1837 frontage register, and writes one prairie_draft structure record per building. A later block is drafted by ADDING rows here (a sheet under `blocks`, its frontages under `frontages`), never by editing the tool. Every number below is a RECONSTRUCTION bounded by the study's starting ranges (RECONSTRUCTION-RULES.md) and recorded as one liberty per block in docs/LIBERTIES.md. A frontage row's `built` (T-3037) is a build year a source prints, carried to the house's record as its `built` claim; the 1911 sheet's reading marks every drafted range's end `to_is: seen`.

fit._doc: How a traced part becomes rectangles: the part is scan-filled on a grid in its lot's own frame, and the largest rectangle inside the fill is taken, then the largest in what is left, until the rectangles cover `coverage` of the fill or `max_rects` are taken. A rectangle smaller than `min_rect_m2` or thinner than `min_side_m` is not taken; one lying `swallowed` or more inside an earlier rectangle of the building is dropped. A frontage row's `front_body_from_u_m` makes a house's first rectangle the largest in front of that lot-frame u (T-2330), for a house the sheet traces in one part with its rear range.

heights._doc: Masonry houses: principal storey 3.9 m and upper storeys 3.5, 3.3 and 3.1 m floor to floor (RECONSTRUCTION-RULES.md: principal 3.2-4.2, upper 2.9-3.7), over a basement whose principal floor stands 1.4 m above grade (the K01 contract's 0.8-1.8). Service buildings: a 3.4 m carriage storey and a 2.8 m loft. A half storey is the roof's: a mansard's 3.0 m lower face, or dormers in a hip.

frontage-28-040.why: 2½B on the map: two full storeys and a half in the roof, read as dormers in a hip behind the stone front.

built.note: The marker: 'Samuel B. Pomeroy Residence. Built 1857'.

frontage-28-041.why: A stone-front house with no named form: the stone-front family's flat roof behind a cornice.

frontage-28-042.why: The register's 'recorded 1886 mansard storey': 3S.B. read as three storeys and the mansard over them.

built.note: The marker: 'Fernando Jones Residence. Built 1866', with a mansard added in 1886.

frontage-28-043.why: Second Empire: slate mansard and dormers over the mapped corner bay.

built.note: The marker: 'Elbridge G. Keith Residence. Built 1870'; the museum's post gives 1870 to 1871.

frontage-28-044.why: Italianate stone front with the register's 'deep bracketed cornice'; 1908 is attached and the census rules the two one building, so one record carries both fronts.

frontage-28-046.why: Chateauesque: the register's 'conical corner turret' and 'steep slate roof'; 2½B read as dormers in the steep hip.

built.note: The marker: 'Byran P. Moulton Residence. Built 1882'.

frontage-28-047.why: 2½S.B. with a 'bay4B': a bay carried a storey above the house, drawn as a corner tower; its corner is not read off the sheet and is reconstructed.

frontage-28-048.skip: The census rules 1936 an alias of 1918 with no footprint of its own (no dwelling drawn on the lot).

frontage-28-049.why: Chateauesque in Bedford stone, not brownstone: the register's 'tall hip/slate roofs, corner tower and conical cap, elaborate gabled dormers' and 'broad curved entry stair'. The tower is drawn at the 18th Street corner, where the corner lot shows it to the intersection; the sheet does not place it, so its corner is reconstructed.

frontage-28-050.why: Romanesque: the register's 'rock-faced brown sandstone front' over 'brick side and rear', so the stone front is brownstone and the walls behind it brick; the steep Romanesque hip stands for the upper gable, whose arched lights are T-1891's.

storeys_1904.note: Two storeys in 1904, where the 1911 sheet reads a '1½-storey brick GARAGE on the alley' (T-3099). The Tribune of 16 April 1904 offers the empty house to rent with a '2 story stable', and the same agents repeat it in September 1905; the Greeley-Carlson plate of 1891 draws a crossed stable marked '25' at the alley behind the house, 38-46 m from the street line where the 1911 sheet's garage stands 37-46 m; and the Chicagology photograph (after 1886; its rights unresolved, so read beside these and not cited for the count) shows it past the house's south flank as a separate pavilion with an arched carriage door under a steep roof. The plan stays the 1911 trace's. Why the 1911 sheet counts one and a half storeys no source says: the stable altered when it became a garage, or its loft counted as a roof storey, are both open.

frontage-28-051.why: The register's 'stone facade, mansard with gabled dormers' and 'projecting bay'; the 1902 Heun alterations are T-1893's to compare.

frontage-28-052.why: The register's 'three-storey wall, high attic/mansard profile, tall chimneys' on a brick body (the map's colour, not the engraving's ashlar); rear2B is the two-storey range.

frontage-28-053.why: The register's 'mansard and dormers, square/pyramidal tower and separate conical bay' and its rule 'preserve both different tower geometries': a square tower under a pyramid at one front corner and a lower round bay under a cone at the other. Which corner carries which is not read off the sheet and is reconstructed.

frontage-28-054.why: The register's post-1887 phase: 'stone-faced Second Empire facade, post-fire upper floor, mansard/dormers, deep cornice, classical portico', the portico drawn as a central entrance.

frontage-28-055.why: Second Empire: the register's 'broad brick/stone mansion, mansard and angular corner bay, dormers' and 'central portico'; the conservatory bay and the 1904 fence are T-1904's and T-1905's.

frontage-28-056.why: 2½S.B.: two full storeys and a half in the roof, read as gabled dormers in a hip over the post-1902 enlargement; the projecting tower/bay is T-1906's. The 1911 sheet's Gatlin Institute is a 1911 use and is not carried back. The sheet traces the house and its rear range as one part, whose largest rectangle is a 47 m strip down the lot; the main body is fitted in front of the part's own break at 21.3 m from the rear lot line, where it narrows to the street front, and the rear range behind it.

built.note: The marker: 'Marshall Field Jr. Residence. Built 1867', enlarged several times, the last in 1902.

frontage-28-057.why: The register's 'restrained masonry villa vocabulary' and its rule 'do not invent a landmark tower': a low hip over the mapped three storeys, no tower.

frontage-28-058.why: The register's 'corner mansion with substantial roof/attic, deep Prairie facade and long 20th Street elevation': a hip with attic dormers over the mapped house, its rear2B range behind.

frontage-20-001.why: 2B brick with the sheet's 'curved bay on the Prairie face': the brick family's hip over two storeys, the bay drawn as a square-cornered projection; nothing stands behind it on the sheet.

frontage-20-002.why: 3B brick, rear 2B: the brick family's hip over three storeys and the two-storey rear range behind.

frontage-20-003.why: 2B brick with a bay on the Prairie face: drawn flat behind a bracketed cornice so that it does not repeat 1600's hip two lots north; which roof it had is T-1859's.

frontage-20-004.why: Italianate stone front: the register's 'smooth ashlar street face, common-brick returns ... arched columned entrance, high stoop, bracketed cornice', the entrance drawn central.

frontage-20-005.why: 2½B brick: two full storeys and a half in the roof, read as dormers in the brick family's hip; the sheet's frame bay at its north-east corner stands as a projection.

frontage-20-006.why: The Robert Law house restored for 1904 (the register's 'irregular earlier brick envelope across lots 13-14, projecting bay, arched windows, stoop, bounded roof'): the plate's L read as the main body and its shallower south part, under a low hip. Its stable on the alley is the sheet's own long two-storey brick building.

frontage-20-007.why: 3B brick, the north half of a pair attached to 1628: the brick family's hip, its entrance at the north end so the pair's doors stand at their outer ends.

frontage-20-008.why: 3B brick, the south half of the pair with 1626: the same family, its entrance mirrored to the south end.

frontage-20-009.why: The register's 'small earlier frame house': 2BB frame read as two storeys under a simple gable with one stack, keeping its small scale between the masonry houses.

frontage-20-010.why: 3B stone-front, attached to 1636 as a pair: the stone-front family's flat roof behind a cornice, the entrance at the pair's middle, beside the party wall: the sheet draws 1634's canted stone bay at the north end of its front and 1636's at the south end of its own, so the pair mirrors (T-2392).

frontage-20-011.why: 3B stone-front, the south half of the pair with 1634: the same family, the one repeated front on the block, which the sheet's attached pair attests. The entrance is at the north end, beside the party wall: the sheet stands the canted stone bay across the south half of the front (T-2348), and 1634's at the north end of its own (T-2392), so the pair mirrors, doors together at the party line.

frontage-20-012.why: The house is the K16 record already standing (see skip); this row names it so its stable keeps its family's id.

frontage-20-013.why: The register's 'paired mirror-image Georgian brick envelope, restrained classical cornice': the north unit of the U-shaped block, the sheet's own north part (p2 of s20fp-1700-b1), under a low hip, its door at the outer (north) end.

frontage-20-014.skip: 1702 is a second number printed on the 1700 front (census alias; study ruling 2): no third house.

frontage-20-015.why: The mirrored partner to 1700 with its own entrance: the south unit (p1 of s20fp-1700-b1) under the same low hip, its door at the outer (south) end, so the pair reads as two houses and one composition.

frontage-20-016.why: The register's 'three-storey/basement brick townhouse with separate entry, cornice, regular sash': flat behind a cornice, attached by a party wall to 1706.

frontage-20-017.why: 2B brick with a stone front: the stone-front family's flat roof behind a cornice.

frontage-20-018.why: The register's Tyrrell/Walker 'Italianate frame': a low hip on deep bracketed eaves over the 2BB frame body, the central stair drawn as a central entrance; the central gable, canted bay and full-width porch are T-1873's.

frontage-20-019.why: 2B brick with a bay: the brick family's hip over two storeys.

frontage-20-020.why: 3B brick, rear 2B, the main block outlined by a dashed line: flat behind a bracketed cornice so that the three brick houses 1726-1736 do not share one roof; which it had is T-1874's.

frontage-20-021.why: The register's 'three-storey brick corner dwelling with bounded mansard/attic treatment' at the 18th Street corner: a mansard over the mapped three storeys.

frontage-20-022.why: 2-storey frame at the 16th Street corner, 'stepped outline' on the sheet: the small frame house's simple gable with one stack (as 1630's across the avenue), the steps standing as the fitted rectangles; its door is on the south, away from the corner's station traffic, and T-1866 reads it.

station.note: The station's dressing is RECONSTRUCTED (T-2399, liberty L-ic-16th-street-station-2399): neither sheet 20 nor Robinson 1886 draws a platform, a canopy, a door or a board, and no picture of this building is known (the Tribune's 1886 'Sixteenth Street Station' sketch is a one-storey depot that the library reads as the C. B. & Q. depot moved away, so it is not built toward). Only the platform's EDGE is read off the sheet: the nearest track's west rail, traced on sheet 20 through the T-1250 fit at 2.05 m off the track wall at the north end and 5.49 m at the south, less 1.0 m of clearance, so the platform tapers from 1.05 m to 4.5 m as the tracks bear away; the canopy stands only where the platform is deeper than it. The wording is the sheet's own lettering of the building, set as a railway's boards.

frontage-20-023.why: Not a house: the sheet letters the two-storey frame building 'ILLINOIS CENTRAL R.R. 16TH ST. STATION' and Robinson 1886 shows a station on the same ground, so the census carries the use to 1904. It stands as the draft's two-storey gabled frame building with its own name and use, dressed as a station by T-2399: a timber platform on the track side, a canopy over it, a passenger door under a hood on the street and lettered nameboards. (The register's '1603' row is this frontage; the sheet prints 1605.)

frontage-20-024.why: The 1904 houses on this frontage are the lot-6 frame pair 1609 and 1611 (block 20's `plates`), each with its own overlay there; the 1911 loft is skipped.

frontage-20-025.why: 4-storey brick, the north half of a pair attached to 1615: four storeys read flat behind a bracketed cornice, a terrace house's roof, its door at the pair's outer (north) end.

frontage-20-026.why: 4-storey brick, the south half of the pair with 1613: the same roof and cornice, its door mirrored to the outer (south) end. The sheet's attached pair attests the repeat.

frontage-20-027.why: 4-storey brick with a stone front and a half-round rear porch: the stone-front family's flat roof behind a cornice; the sheet's stone front stands as its own piece.

frontage-20-028.why: 3B brick, the north unit of an attached group of three (1621-1625): the brick family's hip, its door at the group's north end.

household.name: John H. Hamline's house
household.note: Whose house: John H. Hamline's, built to Treat & Foltz's design of 1885-86 (the left-hand house of the Building Budget drawing, building_budget_1886_06_hamline_farwell_houses), ruled at 1621 by T-2439 on the 1885 permit, the 1884-87 directories, the 1886 occupant map, the 1886 Robinson plate's printed number (robinson_1886_chicago_plate_10) and the 1904 Blue Book, against one 1886 newspaper's '1619' (docs/RESEARCH/hamline-1621-2436/README.md). The front standing here is still the district draft's: T-2440 moves the drawing's build from 1619 to this house.

frontage-20-029.why: 3B brick, the middle unit of the group: flat behind a bracketed cornice so that the group's three fronts are not one repeated face (the study attests the attachment, not a uniform design); which it had is T-1869's.

frontage-20-030.why: 3B brick with a 4-storey rear section, the south unit of the group (the census reads it 3½B): a mansard over the mapped storeys carries the half storey, its door at the group's south end; the rear section stands as the sheet traces it.

frontage-20-031.why: The register's Spalding remodel of the Grosvenor house: 'brick block with steep hip/mansard roof, dormers, tall chimneys, full-height swell bay, projecting gabled wing', drawn as a steep hip with dormers over the 2½B body, the sheet's frame bay as a projection. The 1904 Blue Book lists W. G. Hibbard Jr. at 1637, so the Spalding name is the one provisional association the census keeps; T-1870 rules.

frontage-20-032.why: The register's Italianate mansion with rear addition (the Hibbard house): a low hip on bracketed eaves over the 2½S.B. stone-based body, the half storey as dormers, the 1874 rear range as the sheet traces it; the arched lights, oriel and two-level rear veranda are T-1875's and T-1876's.

built.note: The marker: 'William G. Hibbard Residence. Built 1869'.

frontage-20-033.why: The register's Palmer Kellogg successor: 'irregular three-storey brick envelope, bay projection, rear 2/1-storey ranges, recessed entry, cornice and bounded roof profile', a low hip over the 3B body with the sheet's corner bays as projections. The Boyington/Williams predecessor is excluded (study ruling 10).

frontage-20-034.why: The Dexter house in its post-1889 phase (the register's 'flat classical front, rusticated base, entry portico, upper balcony, cornice and chimneys'): flat behind a cornice, a central entrance. The sheet prints 1721 where the register read 1719; the census rules them one property (study ruling 3), so one house stands and 1719 is its alias.

built.note: The marker: 'Wirt Dexter Residence. Built 1863'. The house was remodelled later.

frontage-20-035.why: The Pullman house, the register's 'brownstone main block, mansard/dormers/cresting, Prairie portico': the Second Empire family's mansard over the 3B stone body, the entrance central on the Prairie front. The east wing's conservatory bay is the K13 record already standing (pullman_house_1729_prairie_conservatory, T-2306), and the porte-cochere, 1892 east addition, stable and glasshouses are T-1880, T-1881 and T-1934's. The draft keeps that record's footprint out of the traced fabric (`keep_out`), so the wing is drawn once; the sheet's two-storey building at the wing's east end (lettered GARAGE, a 1911 use) stands at two storeys (`wing_storeys`), not the house's three.

built.note: The marker: 'George M. Pullman Residence. Built 1870-1876'.

frontage-35-059.why: 3BB frame on a deep lawn at the 20th Street corner (the register's 'painted clapboard, timber sash/eaves and porch'): three storeys under the default low hip, its wings and porches as the sheet traces them; its door is on the north, toward the corner, and 2010, the twin in plan the sheet attests, mirrors it.

frontage-35-060.why: 3BB frame, the twin in plan of 2000 (the register's 'detached dwelling similar to 2000'): the same hip over three storeys, its door mirrored to the south, so the attested pair reads as two houses of one design.

frontage-35-061.why: 3 brick, long and narrow, with a stone bay on its Prairie front: the stone-front family's flat roof behind a cornice, the bay as the sheet's own stone piece.

frontage-35-062.why: 3B with a stone front and a brick rear divided on the diagonal: the stone-front family's flat roof, bracketed so that it does not repeat 2018's plain cornice next door; its door on the south, onto the wide open ground the sheet leaves beside it.

frontage-35-063.why: The Ebenezer Buckingham house at the 21st Street corner (the register's 'mapped substantial brick house, basement, corner-facing elevation'): a low hip over the 3S.B. body with the sheet's bays as projections, the entrance central where the 1888 Inland Architect's portico stands. Its 6-ft walls along 21st Street are not drawn: the draft archetype has no boundary walls, and T-1911 builds them.

frontage-35-064.why: The John B. Sherman house (Burnham & Root, 1874), standing empty in 1904 after Sherman's death: the register's 'steep slate roof and stone dormers' and 'carved chimney tops' as a steep hip with dormers and three stacks over the 3S.B. brick body, the curved stair and clustered columns as a central entrance. The 1911 lettering McCORMICK MEDICAL COLLEGE is a later use and is not drawn; the oriel on its column is T-1919's.

built.note: The marker: 'John B. Sherman Residence. Built 1874'.

frontage-35-065.why: The Mark Kimball house, empty and to let in the spring of 1904 (not W. W. Kimball's at 1801): the register's 'two-storey/basement brick house with simple cornice/roof' as a flat roof behind a plain cornice over the 2B body and its rear range. The to-let notice calls it a stone front and the sheet colours it brick; the draft keeps the sheet's brick, and T-1921 chooses.

frontage-35-066.why: The Harriet Rees house (Cobb & Frost, 1888) at its historical 2110 site, not its present one: the register's 'limestone front, tall gable' as a steep gable whose end faces the avenue over the 3B narrow body and its stone front, two bays wide. Its carved tympanum, loggia and bowed oriel are T-1922's and T-1923's.

frontage-35-067.why: The Rothschild stone-front townhouse: three storeys with a stone front and a rear 2B range, flat behind a bracketed cornice; the sheet's canted bay stands as its stone projection.

frontage-35-068.why: 2-storey brick, a dwelling in 1904 (the 1904 Blue Book lists the Gorton household; DRESS MAKING is the 1911 use): the brick family's low hip over two storeys and its one-storey rear wing; its frame porches stand as the sheet traces them.

works.note: On the target date the house is not finished (census ruling r35-robbins-2126): Robbins bought the Hamill house in 1901 and razed it in 1904, and the May 1905 plate shows the new house complete. The draft therefore stands the working phase the ruling declares, the new house's brick shell partly raised and unroofed on the 1911 footprint, with the alley stable standing. How high the walls stood is RECONSTRUCTED: two of its three storeys and part of the third along the street.

frontage-35-069.why: The Robbins house (Mann, MacNeille & Lindeberg) RISING on 1 July 1904, in the one working phase census ruling r35-robbins-2126 declares: the brick shell two storeys up over its stone basement, the street wall and its returns 1.6 m into the third, openings empty, no roof, a deck at the principal floor and a pole scaffold along the street and the open side. The five-bay front and central entrance are the register's for the finished house (its 'five-bay red-brick front ... fanlit central entry'), laid out as openings only. The May 1905 plate is the finished design and is not read as July 1904 evidence; a 1904 permit or a dated progress photograph replaces this phase (T-1926).

frontage-35-070.why: The Thomas Murdoch house (Cobb, 1890): the register's 'stone-front block with brick rear, prominent rounded street bay/turret with conical cap, 2.5/3-storey transitions': the sheet's 2½ read as dormers in a hip, and a turret under a cone stood on the round bay the sheet draws at the front's north end (its rectangle, fitted from the stone part, is where the turret stands). T-1927 reads its height and cap.

use.name: the three-storey building on the alley behind 2140

frontage-35-071.why: The Tucker/Smith house (Van Osdel, 1876), Byron L. Smith's in 1904: the register's 'mansard/dormers, tall stacks' over the 3S.B. brick body and the sheet's round bay at the 22nd Street corner as a round tower. ONE ROOF STATE, as the register requires: its towers are drawn FLAT-TOPPED AND CRESTED, the house's first state (the pre-1881 stereo, under Tucker's name), because the conical spires are dated only by a 1928 photograph and nothing puts them on the house by 1904; a dated view showing spires by July 1904 replaces this state (T-1928, T-1929). The three-storey building at the alley corner is no one's stable: its 1911 use (CATERER) is not carried back, and it stands as an outbuilding.

built.note: The marker: 'William F. Tucker-Byron L. Smith Residence. Built 1876'.

frontage-35-072.why: 2½B brick with a stone front on the 20th Street corner (W. C. Free's in the 1904 Blue Book, a lead and not an identity): the register's stone-front family is a flat roof, but the sheet's half storey is a roof storey, so the draft takes the default hip with dormers over the stone street face and its traced bay; the door is toward the corner, beside the frame porch the sheet draws on the 20th Street side.

frontage-35-073.why: 3B brick, one of an attached pair with 2005 on a party wall (the census: 'on a party wall with 2005'), with the sheet's curved front bay: three storeys flat behind a bracketed cornice, the rowhouse roof the pair shares; its door at the pair's outer (north) end, mirrored by 2005.

frontage-35-074.why: 3B brick, the second house of the attached pair with 2003: the same bracketed flat roof, its door mirrored to the pair's south end, so the attested pair reads as two houses of one row. Its 16 ft brick wall on the south line is a boundary wall the draft archetype does not draw (T-1912).

frontage-35-075.why: The Max A. Mayer house (Burnham & Root, 1888): the register's 'ogee gable with finial, two attic lights, tall chimneys' on a narrow party-wall front, drawn as the kit's shaped street gable over the 2½B brick body, two bays wide. Its ogee curve, carved frieze and bowed window group are T-1913's and T-1914's; the draft keeps only the silhouette.

built.note: The marker: 'Max A Meyer Residence. Built 1888'.

frontage-35-076.why: The Romanesque neighbour of Mayer (the Lambs' in the 1904 Blue Book): the register's 'rough ashlar front, round-arched entrance, rounded corner turret/conical cap' as the Romanesque family's steep hip with dormers over the 2½B body, and a turret under a cone on the south front corner, where the sheet draws its stone rounded bay. Seen in the 1890s Mayer photograph; T-1915 reads it.

frontage-35-077.why: The William H. Reid house (Beers, Clay & Dutton, 1894): the register's 'heavy cornice, roof balustrade' as a flat roof behind a plain heavy cornice over three storeys, the classical portico as a central entrance. The sheet's 'Fire Proof Construction' is a construction class, not a facade material (census note), and its colour reads as frame on the coarse copy; the record keeps the register's construction. Rustication, surrounds and urns are T-1916's.

frontage-35-078.why: 3B brick with a stone front (the McBeans' in the 1904 Blue Book): the stone-front family's flat roof, bracketed so it does not repeat Reid's plain cornice next door, with the sheet's stone piece as its front bay; the door to the south.

frontage-35-079.why: The James L. High house (built for Benjamin Adams in the late 1870s; High's from 1886, with his 1887 rear range): the register's 'steep main gable, conical rounded corner tower, arched entry' as a steep gable to the avenue over the 2½B body and a round tower under a cone on the north front corner, where the sheet draws its front projection. Its broad side wing's secondary gable is T-1917's.

frontage-35-080.why: 2½B brick on a wide lot, the house the register associates with Silas B. Cobb (an open association, so the id names no one): the villa family's low hip with dormers over the traced body, its frame porch as the sheet draws it, restrained as the register asks ('no borrowed named mansion facade'). T-1917 reads it.

frontage-35-081.why: 2031, the north house of the 1869 Lemont-limestone row (census ruling r35-2031-2035-row; Samuel A. Tolman's in the 1904 Blue Book): the Italianate family's flat roof behind a bracketed cornice over three storeys, its stone street face. The row shares a cornice line and is not three copies, so its doors differ: 2031's north, 2033's south, 2035's toward the corner (T-1918).

frontage-35-082.why: 2033, the Otis homestead in the middle of the 1869 limestone row (Tribune, February 1904): the row's bracketed flat cornice over three storeys and the sheet's full-height canted stone bay, which the fit carries as a bay; the pedimented double-door hood the Walker Evans photograph shows is T-1918's.

frontage-35-083.why: 2035, the 21st Street corner of the 1869 limestone row, Mrs. H. O. Stone's in February 1904: the register's family ('corner of limestone row') matches no draft family, so the row's bracketed flat cornice is set here to keep the shared line; its door toward the corner. Its mixed brick-and-frame rear building stands as the sheet traces it. The census does not read that building's use, so it stands as an outbuilding, not a stable.

frontage-35-084.why: 2½B brick on the 21st Street corner (the Pikes' in the 1904 Blue Book): the brick family's hip with dormers for the half storey over its long rear range, its frame porches as the sheet traces them; its door toward the corner.

frontage-35-085.why: The Robert Roloson house: the register keeps its veranda and mansard tower inferred only once the Armour photograph's orientation agrees, so the draft is the 'constrained plain masonry envelope' it names, a hip over three storeys with the stone front and the one-storey frame veranda the sheet draws on the north and west. T-1924 decides the tower.

frontage-35-086.why: The David Kelley house of 1871, Mrs. Philip D. Armour's in 1904: the register's Second Empire 'patterned slate mansard and cresting' as the family's mansard with dormers over three storeys and a stone street face, the 'central arched doorway and pediment' as a central entrance. Its quoins, paired arches and stepped stair are T-1925's.

built.note: The marker: 'David Kelley-Philip D. Armour Residence. Built 1871'.

frontage-35-087.why: 3B brick with a stone front (Thomas H. Hubbart's in the 1904 Blue Book): the stone-front family's plain flat roof over three storeys and its rear range, the sheet's stone piece as its bay.

frontage-35-088.why: 2BB, a small frame house among brick ones (no household at 2125 in the 1904 Blue Book): two storeys of clapboard under a gable to the avenue, so it reads as the frame dwelling it is, with its one-storey frame range and porches as the sheet traces them, and its crossed frame stable on the alley.

aka: 2129 S. Prairie Avenue (the flats' second number)
frontage-35-089.why: A three-storey brick building of flats, one front under one roof numbered 2127 and 2129 (the sheet's F; census: two flats, not a house): flat behind a bracketed cornice, six bays across its wide front with one central entrance standing for the two numbers; its three-storey frame porch range at the rear as the sheet traces it. T-1931 reads its two doors.

frontage-35-090.why: 2129 is the second number of the 2127 flats (census alias), not a building; the flats carry it.

frontage-35-091.why: 2141 is open ground on the 22nd Street corner (census ruling r35-2141-open-corner): a non-building frontage, so the draft stands nothing on it.

frontage-35x-213.why: The register's red brick and sandstone rowhouse, standing today: flat behind a cornice, the roof its street front shows. The sheet's storey figure is blurred (3 or 4) and is drafted as 3, its neighbour's.

frontage-35x-215.why: The middle rowhouse, set back behind its front yard as the sheet draws it: flat behind a cornice.

register.family: Queen Anne corner rowhouse with gable

frontage-35x-217.why: The corner house, its body the sheet's front part (p1) and its rear range the 3-storey part behind the frame strip: its photographs' gable over the street front, which the sheet's 3½ is, and the copper oriel rising at its Prairie corner to a turret, drawn as the draft's corner turret; the oriel's copper and its corbelled start at the first floor are T-1939's.

frontage-35x-2008.why: The register's brownstone house under a steep hipped roof with tall chimneys (the Inland Architect plate of December 1883): the steep hip in brownstone. notes.function: Second Presbyterian Church (James Renwick, 1872-1874), gutted by fire in March 1900 and rededicated in November 1901 inside its surviving walls and tower (Chicago Tribune, 10 November 1901).
notes.research: The church stands on Michigan Avenue at 20th Street, west of the three committed Sanborn sheets, so it is drafted from HABS IL-328's measured plan and south elevation and placed on the 1904 grid's measured lines. Its 1904 tower state is the full spire: the 1901 Tribune cut and Sloan's photograph (1901-1925) both show it, and it was lost in 1929.
notes.range: The rebuilt church was rededicated in November 1901 (Chicago Tribune, 10 November 1901) and stands today; the draft claims the 1904 target.
notes.position: Michigan Avenue's centre is the e1871 terrain box's reading at 16th Street (E +1136.7), carried south on the bearing of Indiana Avenue's measured east line; its west line is 10.06 m out (the 66 ft every street on the committed sheets prints; Michigan's own width is not read here), and the church's east face stands a reconstructed 3.0 m behind it, as the photograph's lawn strip shows; the south face stands 3.0 m behind East Twentieth Street's measured north line (data/street_grid/1904.json). Good to a few metres.
notes.footprint: The building's whole plan, the nave, the parish hall and the north aisle range as HABS IL-328 sheet 2 draws them, buttresses and the tower's projection left off, so the walls a visitor meets and the ground the context's stand-ins give way to are the church's own; the main body (the nave and narthex, 32.3 x 21.8 m) is draft_plan's first rectangle.
notes.stories: Three draft storeys of 4.6 m over a 0.9 m floor stand the walls to the 14.7 m eave the 1901 cut shows against the nave's ridge; a church has no storeys, and the count only sets the wall height and the rows of openings.
notes.construction: Stone: the rock-faced ashlar of the photograph and the 1901 cut, drawn in stone on HABS IL-328's elevations.
notes.plan: Three rectangles read off HABS IL-328 sheet 2 at its feet bar (the metric bar disagrees by 22 %; the pews' 0.92 m spacing settles which is right): the nave, the parish hall with the chancel rooms beside it, and the north aisle range. The narthex, vestibule and buttresses fold into the rectangles.
notes.elevation: The nave's ridge stands at HABS sheet 4's 87'-8 1/4" (26.7 m: a 48-degree gable over the 21.8 m nave) and the hall's gable at its 80'-1" (24.4 m: 50 degrees over 16.2 m). The tower is HABS sheet 2's 7.9 m square at the south-east corner; its masonry to about 38 m and its spire about 16 m above are proportions read off Sloan's photograph against the nave's ridge (upper figures: the tower stands nearer the camera). Openings are the draft's sash in rows, not the church's lancets, rose and great window, which are T-1942's.

notes.function: The Otis history of 1913 dates the building and its use: Calvary Presbyterian Church laid its corner stone in November 1870, the united First Presbyterian Church finished it after October 1871, and the final service in it was held on 29 December 1912 (otis_1913_first_presbyterian_21st_indiana_1887, pp. 52-56 and 291-292); the 1911 sheet letters it '1st PRESBYN. CHURCH'. So it was the First Presbyterian Church on 1 July 1904.
notes.research: The church fills the 2029-2035 lot on Indiana Avenue at 21st Street: J. C. Cochrane's building for Calvary Church, begun in 1870 and finished by the united First Church about 1872-1873, used until December 1912 (Otis 1913). Sanborn 1911 vol. 3 sheet 35 prints it 48 ft to its eaves with a slated spire marked 90 ft on its south-west tower. The Otis plate of 1887 (otis_1913_first_presbyterian_21st_indiana_1887) shows the west front and the tower whole, and its camera is solved in data/reference_views/first_presbyterian_church_2029_indiana/ (T-3066): the gable, the tower's stages and the spire stand to its heights. It is drafted as a site so that its walls, roof and tower are the church's heights and not a house's; T-3103 dresses the front, the tower and the spire to the plate until it matches; T-3104 reads the book's 1912 plate (otis_1913_first_presbyterian_21st_indiana_1912), whose second camera adds the roof's ventilators, the east gable's stack and the cross's height, and which shows the tower and roof but not the 21st Street flank.
notes.range: Otis 1913 dates the building 1870-1873 and its last service 29 December 1912, so it stands across the 1904 target; the draft's phase keeps the study's 1904-1911 window (study ruling 11).
notes.position: Indiana Avenue's measured east line (data/street_grid/1904.json) with its centre 10.06 m (66 ft) west of it; the church's front stands 2.97 m behind that line and its south face 0.14 m behind 21st Street's north line, the trace's own readings. Good to about the trace's 0.19 m pixel and the sheet's fit.
notes.footprint: The building's whole plan as the trace outlines it: the body with its buttresses, and the tower and porch block that steps south of it at the 21st Street corner; the main body (43.7 x 23.1 m) is draft_plan's first rectangle.
notes.stories: Three draft storeys of 4.6 m over a 0.9 m floor stand the walls to 14.7 m, the sheet's printed 48 ft to the eaves; a church has no storeys, and the count only sets the wall height and the rows of openings.
notes.construction: Brick: the sheet colours it pink.
notes.plan: One rectangle, the body read off the trace in metres from Indiana's line and 21st Street's; the buttresses fold into it and the tower stands as a feature.
notes.elevation: One gable over the body, ridge east-west with its gable to Indiana Avenue, as the Otis 1887 plate shows it (sheet 35 draws dashed hips, which the photograph does not bear out). Through T-3066's camera the gable springs at the north kneeler, 2.0 m in from the body's north wall over a narrow bay with its own flat roof and stack (T-3103), and rises 16.0 m over its 10.6 m half-width to its coping's apex at about 30.9 m, so it stands at 56.5 degrees. The tower is the trace's square at the south-west corner, 6.0 m across its faces, its brick to 39.5 m where the photograph's gablets spring, with the slated octagonal spire out of them. The sheet's printed 90 ft (27.4 m) cannot be the spire's height over grade: the photograph puts the tip at five times the eave's height, the sheet's own 48 ft. T-3103 dresses the front and the tower to the plate (the gothic_church feature; every place, width and height is read off the photograph at 18.7 px/m on the front and 18.2 on the tower, and the match record names each): the coping on its corbel table with kneelers and the cross; the gable's rose, the centre window under a rose head, the two side lancets, the north window and the two small lancets at the north foot, the sill and base courses; the gabled stone porch and its pointed doorway; the tower's pointed door and panel, its two-light window with a rose head, its louvred belfry, its courses, its angle buttresses with their gabled offsets and corner pinnacles, and four gablets; and the spire's taper (5.5 m across at its foot, 3.0 m at the band, 1.1 m at its flat top at 71.8 m), its band of lucarnes at 57.4-59.5 m and the finial's knob, fleur and rod to 78.1 m. What the frontal plate cannot give is reconstructed: the porch's 2.0 m depth, the buttresses' projections, the openings and gablets on the tower's east and north faces (the belfry on all four, the second stage's window on the west and south only, as seen), and the north-west buttress's depth, set 1.5 m proud of the front because its shadow falls on the front wall. The book's 1912 plate (otis_1913_first_presbyterian_21st_indiana_1912; T-3104), taken from Indiana Avenue's roadway about 66 m south of 21st Street looking north-north-east with the camera tilted up, shows the tower's south and west faces, the west gable edge-on with its cross, and the nave's south roof slope to the east gable; it does not show the 21st Street flank, which the low buildings across 21st Street and a streetcar screen below the eaves. Read through its camera it adds: two gabled ventilators on the south slope, about 3.6 m wide, their faces standing on the slope at 23.15 m and rising to about 26.3 m, centred 21.5 m and 32.2 m behind the front; a short stack on the east gable's apex to about 32.4 m; and the cross over the west gable to 34.65 m, where both plates put its top (the 1887 plate's crossbar is the 33.0 m first read as its top). The ventilators' depth into the roof and their faces' material are reconstructed, and the north slope, which neither plate sees, is given none. The 21st Street flank and the rear keep the draft's sash: no picture read so far shows them.
